c.tagline: Zimbabwe's second city of wide colonial avenues and Matobo's granite hills.

taxi.fareNote: Shared minibuses (combis) run fixed routes for small change; metered taxis are rare, so agree a fare before you get in and ride-hailing apps are not established here. Prices are in US dollars; the local ZiG is legal tender too but change often comes back in USD.

emergency.note: 999 is the general emergency line, 995 reaches police and 994 the ambulance service; response can be slow, so private medical-evacuation providers are widely used. 112 also works from mobiles.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

solo.f: generally fine; avoid walking after dark

hood_landmark.Suburbs: Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe, Bulawayo

avoid.reason: No strict no-go zones, but skip the high-density western townships after dark unless accompanied by a local.
Pickpockets and phone-snatchers work the city centre and bus ranks; keep valuables out of sight.

hood_desc: The grid of wide, tree-lined colonial avenues at the heart of town, with City Hall, markets, shops and most budget hotels; walkable and central, the easiest base for first-timers.
A leafy older residential area just east of the CBD (its actual name), full of jacaranda-lined streets, guesthouses and the Natural History Museum nearby; calm and green yet close in.
A quiet, leafy suburb a five-minute drive from the centre with B&Bs, lodges and gardens; relaxed and residential, popular with families and longer-stay visitors.
One of Bulawayo's most exclusive suburbs of large homes on tree-lined streets a few kilometres from the CBD; upscale, spacious and tranquil.
Bulawayo's oldest township, a birthplace of Zimbabwean music and nationalist history and home to the lively Makokoba (Sixth Avenue) market; rich in culture though rough around the edges.

water.note: Chronic shortages and aging pipes make bottled or filtered water the safe choice.

transit.hours: Combis run roughly dawn to early evening; after dark the options thin out and a booked taxi is the safest choice.
transit.note: Bulawayo has no metro, tram or formal city bus network. Shared minibuses (combis, or 'emergency taxis') cover the main routes from the city-centre ranks, supplemented by private taxis.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the conductor, usually in small US-dollar notes; the local ZiG is also accepted. There is no transit card.

bus: Long-distance coaches to Harare, Victoria Falls and Johannesburg (Intercape, Pathfinder, CityLink)
Shared combis to Matobo, Gwanda and regional towns
train: Overnight National Railways of Zimbabwe sleeper train to Victoria Falls; a slow line also runs to Harare

transit.m: Taxi or hotel shuttle to the city centre (25-30 min); there is no scheduled airport bus

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants; small change for guides and drivers is appreciated.

food.name: Sadza with oxtail stew
food.desc: Zimbabwe's white maize staple, stiff and steaming, served with slow-braised oxtail in rich gravy. Eaten by hand, rolled into a ball and dipped.

places.name: The Cattleman Restaurant
places.note: Long-running Bulawayo grill house where the sadza-and-stew plates come with proper Matabeleland beef.

places.name: Cape to Cairo
places.note: Landmark bar-restaurant with a daily local menu; oxtail and sadza is the plate regulars order.

places.name: Garden Bistro
places.note: Central all-day eatery with generous traditional plates and a shaded courtyard.

food.name: Braai beef and boerewors
food.desc: Bulawayo is cattle country, and the braai is a weekend institution: thick T-bones and coils of spiced boerewors sausage grilled over open coals.

places.name: The Cattleman Restaurant
places.note: The city's best-known steakhouse; ask for the mixed grill with wors.

places.name: Banff Lodge Hotel
places.note: Leafy suburban hotel with a popular weekend braai and garden seating.

places.name: Cresta Churchill Hotel
places.note: Reliable hotel grill on the road out to the Matobo Hills; good stop before or after a park day.

food.name: Biltong
food.desc: Air-dried, coriander-spiced strips of beef or game. Zimbabweans buy it by the bag for road trips; wet or dry, sliced or in chunky sticks.

places.name: Ascot Shopping Centre butcheries
places.note: Cluster of butchers cutting biltong and droewors to order; the everyday local source.

places.name: Bulawayo City Hall car park market
places.note: Open-air stalls selling bagged biltong alongside crafts and produce.

places.name: Haddon and Sly food hall
places.note: Historic downtown store with a deli counter handy for takeaway snacks.

food.name: Amacimbi (mopane worms)
food.desc: Matabeleland's most famous delicacy: mopane caterpillars, dried then fried with onion, tomato and chilli. Chewy, smoky and deeply protein-rich.

places.name: Makokoba Market
places.note: Bulawayo's oldest township market; the classic place to buy amacimbi by the cup.

places.name: Renkini Bus Terminus stalls
places.note: Busy terminus food stalls frying amacimbi and serving them with sadza.

places.name: Ingwebu Tavern
places.note: Rustic municipal tavern where traditional relishes are served with opaque beer.

food.name: Umfushwa with peanut butter
food.desc: Sun-dried leafy greens rehydrated and stirred with thick peanut butter, the Ndebele relish that turns a plate of sadza into a proper meal.

places.name: Makokoba Market
places.note: Sacks of dried greens and freshly ground peanut butter from the same aisle.

places.name: Dickies Restaurant
places.note: No-frills local kitchen doing big-portion sadza plates with traditional vegetable relishes.

places.name: The Deck
places.note: Serves indigenous vegetables alongside grilled meats for a mixed traditional plate.

food.name: Amagwinya (fat cakes)
food.desc: Golf-ball-sized deep-fried dough, crisp outside and pillowy in, sold hot from morning until dusk. Eaten plain, or split around polony or jam.

places.name: Egodini area vendors
places.note: Commuter-hub vendors frying them fresh from dawn; the cheapest breakfast in town.

places.name: Renkini Bus Terminus stalls
places.note: Fat cakes handed over hot in newspaper to travellers boarding country buses.

places.name: Makokoba Market
places.note: Rows of vendors with bubbling pots; good with a cup of sweet tea.

food.name: Maheu
food.desc: Thick, lightly fermented non-alcoholic maize drink, sold chilled in cartons or ladled from home-made batches. Faintly sour, filling and refreshing.

places.name: Makokoba Market
places.note: Home-made maheu poured by the cup, sweeter and tangier than the shop version.

places.name: Ascot Shopping Centre
places.note: Supermarkets and kiosks stock chilled cartons in maize, banana and pineapple flavours.

places.name: Egodini area vendors
places.note: Street sellers pair it with fat cakes for a cheap workday breakfast.

food.name: Ingwebu opaque beer
food.desc: Bulawayo's own municipal brew: a cloudy, porridge-like sorghum beer drunk from shared plastic pots. Tart, low in alcohol and unmistakably local.

places.name: Ingwebu Tavern
places.note: Council-run beer garden pouring the city's traditional brew straight from the source.

places.name: Makokoba beer gardens
places.note: Historic township drinking halls; lively, sociable and cheap.

places.name: Cape to Cairo
places.note: Central bar option if you would rather have a cold Zambezi lager alongside.

landmarks: Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe
One of Africa's finest museums displays over 75,000 specimens, including a famous mounted elephant among the largest ever taken, plus rich mineral and history halls.
National Railway Museum
Steam locomotives, vintage coaches and Rhodes' private saloon car recall Bulawayo's heyday as southern Africa's great railway junction.
Bulawayo City Hall and Centre
The colonial-era City Hall anchors a grid of streets famously built wide enough to turn a full ox-cart team, lined with faded Victorian and Art Deco facades.
National Gallery Bulawayo (Douslin House)
Housed in an elegant 1901 building, the gallery showcases contemporary Zimbabwean painting and sculpture with artists' studios on its upper floor.
Chipangali Wildlife Orphanage
A long-running sanctuary on the city's edge cares for orphaned and injured lions, leopards and antelope, offering close encounters with rescued wildlife.
Nesbitt Castle
An eccentric Edwardian granite castle in the Hillside suburb, complete with turrets and battlements, now operating as a boutique hotel and tea stop.
Centenary and Central Parks
Adjoining parks shade the city center with jacarandas, fountains, a miniature railway and picnic lawns, hosting the annual trade fair crowds.
Hillside Dams Conservancy
Two restored colonial-era dams amid aloe gardens and granite outcrops form a tranquil birdwatching and walking reserve minutes from downtown.
Mzilikazi Arts & Crafts Centre
A working craft hub in Mzilikazi Township since 1963, where sculptors, weavers and potters create and sell traditional Ndebele art and pottery.
St Mary's Cathedral (Basilica)
A Gothic-style Catholic cathedral raised to minor basilica status in 2013, its twin spires anchoring the west end of downtown Bulawayo's 9th Avenue.

dom.op: National Railways of Zimbabwe — tickets at Bulawayo station, no online booking

train.note: No working international trains - the services to Botswana and South Africa have long been suspended. Domestically, NRZ runs the overnight Bulawayo-Victoria Falls train, which is slow, basic and much loved by railway enthusiasts, plus the Harare service. Both are subject to breakdowns and long delays. Tickets are sold at the station on the day; there is no online booking. Bulawayo also has the excellent National Railways Museum.

intl.to: Johannesburg (South Africa) - via the Beitbridge or Plumtree/Botswana border

intl.op: regional coach operators — tickets at the Bulawayo terminal

bus.note: Bulawayo is closer to the Botswana border at Plumtree than to Beitbridge, so some Johannesburg services route through Botswana instead, which is often quicker. Carry your passport and cash for border fees. Domestic coaches reach Harare in about 6 hours and Victoria Falls in 6-7, considerably faster than the train.

ferry.note: Zimbabwe is landlocked and Bulawayo is inland in Matabeleland, so there are no ferries. The Kariba ferry operates on Lake Kariba in the north, and the Zambezi at Victoria Falls has sunset cruises rather than transport.

half.name: Matobo National Park
half.blurb: A UNESCO landscape of balancing granite kopjes, San rock art and rhino tracking, where Cecil Rhodes chose his grave at panoramic World's View.

half.name: Khami Ruins
half.blurb: The UNESCO-listed stone capital that succeeded Great Zimbabwe rises in terraced granite platforms above the Khami River, twenty kilometers west of the city.
